The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00124

At first, the Murji'ites remained politically neutral between right and left. Their social origins were quite different from those of the classes that made up the left. It is telling that it was Nafi ibn al-Azraq, the most radical of the leaders of the far left — the Kharijites — who first gave them the name Murji'ites. They had stood aside when Muslims fell out with one another towards the end of Uthman's rule. They took no part in the revolt against him; nor, after his death, did they join Muawiya ibn Abi Sufyan and the supporters of Uthman in seeking to avenge him. Instead, they cautiously waited to see how the struggle would turn out.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00125

It is extremely difficult to trace the origins of this opportunistic neutrality. The earliest writings setting out Murji'ite beliefs are lost. Their later books have not survived either, because the movement was persecuted during the Abbasid age — the very age when the history of Islam was being written down.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00126

The books of the Kharijites and the Shia are full of stories, traditions and sayings attributed to the Prophet — some fabricated or falsely attributed — in which one can glimpse the first seeds of their ideas, before they emerged as political parties. We have no similar accounts to shed light on the origins of Murji'ite thought. Ahmad Amin, however, suggested that signs of this way of thinking could already be found among some of the Prophet's earliest companions, such as Abu Bakra, Abd Allah ibn Umar, Imran ibn Husayn and others who remained neutral in the conflict that broke out towards the end of Uthman's caliphate. Amin bases his argument on a saying of the Prophet reported by Abu Bakra:
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00128

There will be times of civil strife. The one who sits still will be better off than the one who walks, and the one who walks will be better off than the one who rushes into it. When it comes, let those who have camels go to their camels, those who have sheep go to their sheep, and those who have land go to their land.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00129

In Amin's view, then, this neutrality had a religious basis: uncertainty about where the right lay in a difficult dispute. He believed that this attitude continued to guide the Murji'ites during the Great Civil War, and drew on an account given by Ibn Asakir:
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00131

The doubters were those who had been away on military campaigns. When they returned to Medina after Uthman was killed, they found that the people, whom they had last known to be united and free of disagreement, were divided. They said, “We left you united, without a quarrel among you. We have come back to find you at odds. Some of you say that Uthman was killed unjustly, and that he and his supporters had the stronger claim to justice. Others say that Ali and his supporters were in the right. We trust them all and believe them. We will not disown or curse either of them, nor testify against them. We leave their case to God, so that God himself may judge between them.”
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00132

It seems that Amin was influenced in forming this view by Goldziher, who suggested that “the way the Murji'ites thought can be traced back to a moderate view that emerged in an earlier age ... They took no part in the dispute and left it to God to judge the matter.”
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00133

It seems to us that this neutrality, arising from doubts about which side was in the right, does not really describe the Murji'ites. It applies instead to a number of leading companions of the Prophet, such as Abd Allah ibn Umar and Saad ibn Abi Waqqas, who wanted no part in the dispute and preferred to keep their religious lives free of it. The Murji'ites, by contrast, kept out of it, I believe, because they wanted to stay safe in this world and protect their own interests. One group among them, as the saying of the Prophet quoted above suggests, thought it wiser to look after their worldly affairs, their farms and their flocks. Another group had been loyal to Uthman before his death and did not join the rebels. But they did not side with Muawiya either, for fear of endangering their interests, since at first the struggle seemed to be going Ali's way. This is apparent from the account by Ibn Asakir quoted earlier.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00134

Their neutrality was a cautious, calculated wait for an opportunity. When the struggle left Ali in a weaker position and Muawiya's star began to rise, they were quick to come to his aid. They recognised the legitimacy of his caliphate and justified the rule of whoever held power. Al-Nawbakhti was therefore entitled to brand them as “the Hashwiyya [a disparaging label], followers of kings and helpers of whoever prevails. They were called Murji'ites because they befriended all the conflicting parties and claimed that everyone who prayed towards Mecca was a believer, provided they openly professed the faith.”
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00135

We can find evidence of this in the sources. The first group included those whom al-Khayyat called the Nawabit — in his words, “supporters of Uthman who believed that human actions were predetermined and that judgement should be deferred.” The other group included people like Ghaylan ibn Abi Ghaylan of Damascus. His father had been a client of Uthman ibn Affan and joined Muawiya in Syria when the latter secured the caliphate. Because both groups were opportunists seeking to advance themselves, al-Zabidi called them Hashwiyya. As al-Nawbakhti says, the Hashwiyya are followers of kings and supporters of whoever comes out on top.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00136

When Muawiya won the struggle, the Murji'ites followed him and became a pillar of his rule. They put their beliefs to work in justifying his caliphate and persuading Muslims to obey him. Their view of what happens to a person who commits a grave sin makes this clear. The Kharijites declared such a person an unbeliever. The Mu'tazilites held that the person occupied a position somewhere between belief and unbelief. The Murji'ites, however, refused to pass judgement, leaving the matter to God. (This principle of deferring judgement is known as irja.) In taking this view, they stood apart from all the opposition parties, which regarded the Umayyads as having seized the caliphate unlawfully.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00137

They also held that faith consisted in affirming belief in words, not in deeds. In other words, what a person does is neither an essential part of faith nor included in its meaning. This explains how the Murji'ites could refrain from opposing rulers and submit to them without believing that their own faith suffered in any way from such passivity. The Kharijites took the opposite view: they believed it was essential to oppose their enemies, in keeping with the principle of “enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong”.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00138

The Murji'ites held that “any sin short of worshipping other gods alongside God can be forgiven, and if a person dies believing in the oneness of God, the sins and wrongs they have committed will not harm them”. Here we have a clear justification for the Umayyads' seizure of the right to rule by deceit, assassination, bribery and intimidation. For this reason, deferring judgement was the “religion of kings”. Unlike the other religious movements, the Murji'ites did not oppose the Umayyad government. Instead, they recognised its legitimacy and called for obedience to it, “and that in itself was support enough”.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00139

This helps explain why the Umayyads dealt so ruthlessly with every Islamic religious movement except the Murji'ites. There can be little doubt that the early Umayyad rulers looked after the leaders of this school. Some lived in Damascus, even as the leaders of other movements suffered persecution and all manner of torture. The Kharijites faced such harsh treatment at the hands of the governors of Iraq that they were forced to shift their activity eastwards. The Shia in Kufa, meanwhile, were persecuted and made to help their governors fight the Kharijites. The aim was to set the two movements against each other, weaken both and rid the Umayyads of their bitterest enemies in one stroke.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00140

The Murji'ite leaders enjoyed a peaceful life in Basra, free from harassment by its governors. They set about spreading their beliefs among the city's people. Hassan ibn Bilal al-Muzani was the first to preach the doctrine there, and his message was warmly received. The people of Basra found in the idea of deferring judgement just what they had been looking for. They were weary of war. After the horrors of the battles of the Camel, Siffin and al-Nukhayla, they longed for safety and peace. Murji'ite teaching gave their desire to live quietly and avoid further conflict a religious justification. It also served as an antidote to the excesses of the radical movements, whose beliefs had little appeal to them. Small wonder that most turned to the Murji'ites and “occupied themselves with their own affairs”, regardless of the kind of government in power. By the standards of their faith, that government was neither a rebel nor a government that had gone astray. All this brings out the concern for practical advantage, in the spirit of the philosopher Jeremy Bentham, that characterised the Murji'ites while they defended the existing order — or, at the very least, a tendency to put their own interests above all else. It is a familiar feature of parties of the centre in every age.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00141

The Murji'ites could not remain loyal to the right for long, however. Anger against the Umayyads soon reached boiling point, and social problems grew ever more acute. The successors of the devout caliph Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz turned their backs on the reforms he had introduced. The left — the Kharijites and the Shia — struck ever harder, despite the ruthless repression of the Umayyads. The dynasty's downfall now looked inevitable. The Murji'ites sensed that the tide was turning in favour of the left. They turned with it and sympathised with the new movements fighting for justice.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00142

Ideas that had once justified the existing order now became a programme of reform, in tune with the new realities of society. Naturally, reform became the defining feature of Murji'ite thought in this period. They called for “putting the Quran and the Prophet's teachings into practice and adopting the principle of consultation in government”. What, then, were the defining features of this new phase, in its ideas, its social basis and its political activity?
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00143

In the world of ideas, we see Murji'ite beliefs taking a revolutionary turn. They were influenced by the Kharijites and the Shia, who called for revolt against injustice. They also adopted some of the Qadarites' ideas about human freedom. The mawali, the non-Arab Muslims living under Arab patronage, flocked to the movement and became the main force behind this new form of Murji'ite belief. This was a momentous social change, and it had far-reaching political consequences: the Murji'ites took part in movements against the Umayyads, including those led by Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Ashath and Yazid ibn al-Muhallab.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00144

We believe this change began in the 60s of the first century AH and was centred on the city of Kufa, just as Basra had earlier been the centre of the movement's defence of the established order. Kufa offered ideal conditions for the growth of the Murji'ites' new ideas. The different religious schools competed in an atmosphere of learning and tolerance. Their leaders debated and tested their ideas against one another in “an environment that respected knowledge, the demands of religious law and the rules of reasoned thought”. The Murji'ites were able to draw on these schools as they developed their new outlook.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00145

They joined all the opposition parties in holding that the leadership of the Muslim community could only be established by the agreement of the community as a whole. That meant denying the Umayyads the right to rule, since not everyone recognised the legitimacy of their caliphate. The Murji'ites borrowed the democratic political ideas of the Kharijites, declaring that someone outside the tribe of Quraysh could legitimately lead the community and that anyone who upheld the Quran and the Prophet's teachings had the right to do so.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00146

They also abandoned their earlier beliefs, which had separated deeds from faith in order to justify the established order. Following the Kharijites and the Qadarites, they now insisted that action was essential to faith: a believer had to stand up against wrongdoing and seek to put things right. “Whoever has truly and sincerely surrendered to God in their heart and loves Him will not disobey Him by committing a sin.” Action, then, is inseparable from faith and flows naturally from it, especially since, according to their belief, “faith neither increases nor decreases”. In its new form, Murji'ite teaching thus set a higher standard for faith, one that demanded action. This made the Murji'ites, in the words of a modern scholar, a strict religious school. We can trace the roots of this strictness to the Kharijites, who insisted on enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. Perhaps it was this convergence between the two schools that led people to call the Murji'ites of that period “the Kharijite Murji'ites”.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00147

The Murji'ites were also influenced by Shia thought. From the Shia they adopted the principle of interpreting religious texts beyond their literal meaning, which gave them a degree of flexibility in adapting to the changing realities of society. They also drew on the ideas of taqiyya (concealing one's beliefs under threat) and the awaited Mahdi, the leader expected to restore justice. We will examine both in more detail later. Some Murji'ite leaders, indeed, were quite willing to profess Shia sympathies openly for political reasons. They also sympathised with the Prophet's family in spite of the brutal repression of the Umayyad governors.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00148

The Murji'ites had no qualms about adopting some of the ideas of the Qadarites, the forerunners of the Mu'tazilites, and turning their backs on their own earlier beliefs. “They gave up the belief that people have no choice in their actions in favour of human freedom, and forged a close bond between faith and reason.” This is clear from the following statement:
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00150
Faith concerns what reason tells us must be done. What reason tells us we may leave undone is no part of faith.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00151

Both action and reasoned thought were thus necessary to faith. Merely believing in the oneness of God without thinking it through did not amount to faith. Some Murji'ite groups also adopted the Qadarites' belief that the Quran was created rather than eternal. It is hardly surprising that some scholars of the Islamic religious movements confused the Murji'ites with the Mu'tazilites, calling them “the Mu'tazilite Murji'ites”. Mistaken though this was, it shows just how deeply Mu'tazilite thought had influenced the movement at this stage.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00152

In short, in its new revolutionary form, the Murji'ite movement had become the third party opposing the Umayyad caliphate, alongside the Kharijites and the Shia. Its once moderate views had become radical, and the very principles it had once used to justify the established order had become revolutionary. So much so that al-Nakhai declared: “Given their numbers, I fear the Murji'ites pose a greater danger to this community than the Azariqa.” And the Azariqa, as we know, were the most radical and revolutionary of all the Kharijite groups.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00153

The movement could never have become a revolutionary force until the mawali embraced it. They joined the opposition parties because they wanted to give their revolt a legitimate basis in religious principles. They were divided among the three opposition parties. Ibn Saad gives us a revealing account of this:
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00155
The jurist Ibn Abi al-Jad al-Ghatafani had a client with six sons. Two were Shia, two were Murji'ites, and two held the views of the Kharijites.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00156

The mawali of Kufa were the first to take up Murji'ite beliefs. They learned them from their Arab patrons, who were at odds with the Umayyad government because it favoured the Arabs of Syria over those of Iraq. Some leaders of the Iraqi Arabs therefore turned to revolt in their struggle for equal treatment. They spread the same demand among their Persian clients under the banner of the Murji'ite movement. Muhammad ibn al-Ashath ibn Qays, himself a Murji'ite, was bitterly opposed to the Umayyads and fought against them in the ranks of Musab ibn al-Zubayr. His son Abd al-Rahman inherited that bitterness and went on to lead the famous revolt that we will examine shortly.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00157

Umar ibn Qays al-Masir learned Murji'ite teachings from Muhammad ibn al-Ashath and spread them among the mawali. Dharr ibn Abd Allah ibn Zurara al-Hamdani, who inherited his father's hatred of the Umayyads and their governors in Iraq, and Amr ibn Murra ibn Abd Allah al-Murari were also leading figures in spreading Murji'ite beliefs among the mawali of Kufa. It was from Iraqi Arabs such as these that the mawali of Kufa learned the doctrines of the movement. Qays al-Masir, a captive from Daylam and a client of Ali ibn Abi Talib, was the first of the city's mawali to embrace them. His son Umar, a client of the Thaqif tribe, learned the beliefs from him. He studied their fundamental principles and their details so thoroughly that he became the leader of the Murji'ite group known as the Masiriyya. Ubayd al-Muktib, leader of the Ubaydiyya group, was a client of the Dabba tribe. Ghassan of Kufa, head of the Ghassaniyya group, was also one of the mawali. He lived at the same time as Abu Hanifa and was said to hold views similar to his.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00158

Kufa had thus become the centre of the new Murji'ite movement. Here, the hopes of the mawali for an end to the injustices of Umayyad rule came together with the Iraqi Arabs' desire to be treated on an equal footing with the Arabs of Syria. It was natural that many of the Murji'ites of Basra, angered by the policies of al-Hajjaj, would move to Kufa. Once they had grown strong enough, they turned to revolt.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00159

There is no shortage of evidence that the Murji'ites took part in the revolt of Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Ashath (80–84 AH). Among their leaders who joined it were Amir al-Shabi, Muhammad ibn al-Saib al-Kalbi and Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla. Great numbers of the mawali also fought alongside the Iraqi Arabs in Ibn al-Ashath's army, known as the “Army of Peacocks”, which comprised a hundred thousand Arabs and as many mawali. The Murji'ites pledged their allegiance to Ibn al-Ashath on the basis of “the Book of God and the teachings of His Prophet, and the removal of leaders who have gone astray”.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00160

The rebels gathered in Kufa and defeated the armies of al-Hajjaj in several battles. The caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan tried to win over the Arabs with concessions that excluded the mawali. He offered to dismiss al-Hajjaj, give the Iraqi Arabs the same state allowances as the people of Syria, and let Ibn al-Ashath govern a province of his choice. But the mawali insisted that the caliph himself must go. The caliph therefore sent troops from Syria to reinforce al-Hajjaj, who defeated the rebels at Dayr al-Jamajim, outside Kufa, and killed many of them. He forced the prisoners to declare themselves unbelievers, and many did so out of fear and to conceal their true beliefs.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00161

Ibn al-Ashath's revolt was more than a clash between Iraq and Syria, as Wellhausen believed. Nor was it merely a struggle between the Qaysi and Yemeni tribal groupings, or simply the product of one man's ambitions. We cannot overlook the part played by the mawali, who rose up demanding equal access to state allowances and the right to be included on the official register of those receiving them. All these groups shared one aim: opposition to Umayyad rule. Murji'ite teaching, now transformed into a revolutionary creed, was the religious bond that held them together. This was, then, a social revolution clothed in religious language. Perhaps that explains why al-Hajjaj insisted that the defeated rebels declare themselves unbelievers and was so determined to drive the mawali out of Kufa and send them back to their home regions. Ibn Abd Rabbih reports that al-Hajjaj berated them, saying: “You are foreign barbarians, non-Arabs; your own villages are where you belong.” He then broke up their communities and sent them wherever he pleased, marking each man's hand with the name of the town to which he was being sent.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00162

Just as the Murji'ites joined the coalition led by Ibn al-Ashath against the Umayyads, they played much the same role in supporting the movement of Yazid ibn al-Muhallab (100–102 AH). They gave this revolt a revolutionary character, socially as well as religiously. The similarities between the two revolts are striking. Personal motives played a part in Ibn al-Muhallab's movement, too, given the hostility between him and the caliph Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik. The rivalry between the Qaysis and the Yemenis was also very much in evidence: Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik had cut the Yemenis' allowances to half what the Qaysis received. Great numbers of mawali in southern Iraq joined the revolt. It received the blessing of prominent Murji'ites such as al-Sumayda al-Kindi, Abu Ru'ba and Thabit Qutna, who were followed by the mass of Iraq's Murji'ites.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00163

Murji'ite principles were plainly reflected in the demands of the revolt: justice and equality, an end to obedience to the Umayyad caliph, and a return to government by consultation. Ibn al-Muhallab received pledges of allegiance based on the Book of God and the teachings of His Prophet. He managed to take Basra and the adjoining areas of Persia and Ahwaz, but was soon defeated and killed when the caliph sent his Syrian armies against him. The Murji'ites suffered severe persecution and brutal repression, and their leaders endured the harshest ordeals.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00164

It had become clear that the Murji'ite doctrine, once a source of support for the Umayyad government, had turned into a cause that gave its backing to movements against it. The government went to great lengths to hunt down the Murji'ites and wipe them out, especially under Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik, who imposed a harsh governor on Iraq, Khalid ibn Abd Allah al-Qasri. Hisham also persecuted the Murji'ite leaders in Syria, putting some of them to death, including Ghaylan of Damascus. Khalid followed much the same course, killing Murji'ites and pursuing the remnants of the movement. He is said to have personally slaughtered al-Jad ibn Dirham, a prominent figure of the movement, on the morning of the Feast of Sacrifice, like a sheep being sacrificed.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00165

After these ordeals, the Murji'ites had to change the way they carried on their struggle, and they did indeed begin to adopt a new policy. It seems to us that this policy had two main aims. The first was to try to bring about a transformation of the caliphate in Syria, winning the caliphs over to their beliefs and persuading them to pursue a policy of reform. The second was to build an organised underground movement in Khurasan, following the example of the Shia and the Kharijites. It seems that they worked with the Mu'tazilites towards the first of these goals, while drawing on the Hashemite movement to achieve the second. We know that the ideas of the Murji'ites in Syria had come very close to those of the Mu'tazilites. They persuaded the caliph Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz to abandon the policies of his predecessors and place Arabs and mawali on an equal footing in their rights and obligations. They also guided the caliph al-Walid ibn Yazid in his efforts to revive the policies of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz after the latter's reforms had been undone following his death. Small wonder: al-Walid sought the friendship of the Qadarites and the Murji'ites and acted on the advice of their leaders.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00166

The caliph Marwan ibn Muhammad, too, sought to tackle the mounting problems of his reign in a spirit of reform. He drew close to the Murji'ites and courted their leaders. He is even said to have embraced their beliefs, learning them from his tutor al-Jad ibn Dirham, which earned him the name Marwan al-Jadi. Perhaps the appeal of the Murji'ite movement to the last Umayyad rulers can be explained by their desire to delay the downfall of their state. They hoped to enlist the help of the centre against the threat from the left. With this in mind, Wellhausen was quite right to say that “the devout and God-fearing rebels had gained a firm foothold and grown stronger in Syria”.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00167

Yet a policy of reform could not achieve its aims. The situation called for a revolution on a far greater scale. The underground movements of the Shia and the Kharijites were already making their influence felt in the eastern and western parts of the state, and in the south as well. The Murji'ites followed the example of both in organising underground. At first they tried to make Iraq the centre of their activity. They turned to Basra, their old stronghold from the days when they had defended the established order, but their message found little support there.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00168

The Murji'ites then looked east, where the movement in support of the Prophet's family was spreading among the mawali. They took a similar path, adapting their religious beliefs to the circumstances of underground activity and drawing on Shia political thought. They held that a person who believed in their heart was a Muslim believer, even if they outwardly professed Judaism or Christianity. This was clearly the idea of taqiyya, concealing one's true beliefs when necessary. They also endorsed interpretation beyond the literal meaning of religious texts and “reading disputed passages in a figurative sense”. This gave them the flexibility to adapt their positions to changing circumstances and the needs of the moment. They took up the idea of the awaited Mahdi, too, saying he would appear to tear down the walls of Damascus and bring Umayyad rule to an end. They were preaching, even before the Abbasids, the coming of the man with the black banners, who would rise in the East and fill the earth with justice after it had been filled with oppression. Black banners had long been associated with the fight against injustice and aggression, going back to the days of the Prophet.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00169

Whereas the Abbasid movement called for an agreed-upon leader from the family of Muhammad, the Murji'ites called for one whom the Muslims at large could agree on. This made their cause more popular. In this respect, it was closer to the “democracy” of the Kharijites than to the rule of a small elite in the Hashemite movement, which reserved the right to lead the community for the Prophet's family alone.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00170

The efforts of Murji'ite advocates in the East therefore met with success. People flocked to Abd Allah al-Jamali al-Muradi, one of their advocates, and Abu Muawiya the Blind enjoyed the same success as his predecessor. The people of Jurjan gathered around Jawwab ibn Abd Allah al-Taymi of Kufa and learned the basic principles of the faith from him. By far the most famous of these advocates was Jahm ibn Safwan. He is credited with completing the spread of the movement in Khurasan, to such an extent that Murji'ite beliefs there came to be associated with his name. He was himself from Khurasan — either Tirmidh or Samarkand, it is said. He embraced Islam and settled in Kufa as a client of the Banu Rasib of the Azd tribe. He learned the more developed form of Murji'ite teaching from al-Jad ibn Dirham, and held that the Quran was created and that human beings were responsible for their own actions, in opposition to those who relied on the sayings of the Prophet and the traditions handed down from earlier generations.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00171

Jahm had long debates with the leaders of other religious schools in Khurasan. He came out on top, “which drew people towards him”. He began spreading Murji'ite beliefs in Tirmidh, then moved to Balkh. He made contact with al-Harith ibn Surayj, who had come forward to lead the revolt against the Umayyads in Khurasan. Jahm became his secretary and the leading voice of his cause, reading his letters aloud at public gatherings and urging people to support his stand against Umayyad rule. Thanks to his efforts, the mawali embraced the beliefs of the Murji'ites and joined al-Harith's revolt. And so, before the second century AH was over, Murji'ite beliefs had come to dominate the eastern regions of the Umayyad state. Wellhausen was right to say that in Khurasan the movement was a way of bringing people together. It was above all a moral reaction against the outward show of Islam that passed for the religion of the Arab government at the time.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00172

The Murji'ites raised inspiring demands: equality regardless of tribal ties or ethnic origins, and a return to the practice of Islamic law, founded on tolerance and consent rather than the violence and bloodshed associated with the Kharijites.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00173

That is why the people of Khurasan rallied around al-Harith ibn Surayj, who recruited seventy thousand of them and drew on their support in launching his famous revolt. We need not dwell on the sequence of events. What matters more for our purposes is understanding the motives, nature and aims of the revolt.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00174

We disagree with Ahmad Amin's view that the revolt arose out of tribal disputes and personal feuds. Tribal rivalry played no part whatsoever in a movement whose character was wholly social and religious. Arabs and mawali stood side by side in it, fighting against Arab supremacy and drawing their inspiration from Islam. It was in the name of Islam that the revolution took up the cause of justice, once the Umayyad government had strayed from the path of Islamic law. It gave voice to a revolutionary Islam, one that made those principles the very grounds on which it challenged the existing system of government. The rebels called on people to fight for God's cause against the Umayyads and their officials, and for justice against tyranny and oppression. Religious scholars came forward to urge the people to join what they regarded as a legitimate revolution and keep its spirit alive. They would say:
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00176
Fight them, and do not feel guilty for killing them if you act with sincere conviction. Fight them for their sins, for the injustice of their rule and for their tyranny in matters of religion.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00177

Nor was this simply an ethnic uprising in which Arabs fought Persians. The oppressed classes of both peoples came together against the Arab aristocracy of Khurasan and the members of the old Persian aristocracy who supported it. Among the rebels were dissident Arabs from the frontier cavalry and the educated religious class, the scholars of Islamic law, drawn from both the Qaysi and Yemeni groupings. Alongside them were small landowners from among the mawali and villagers who were impoverished peasants. On the other side stood the Umayyad Arab troops in Khurasan and the Persian landowning class known as the dahaqin, who formed the backbone of the Umayyad administration. The dividing line between the rebels and their enemies — between what the rebels saw as God's army and the government's army — was therefore a matter of class.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00178

Personal ambition also falls away as an explanation once we understand the character of al-Harith ibn Surayj, the leader of the revolt. He was not driven by ambitions of his own, nor did he dream of achieving worldly glory for himself. The historical sources depict him as a devout Muslim, a man of simple habits and a reformer who devoted his life to the defence of justice. He had once fought the Turks in the ranks of the Muslims, when the war was a jihad. Later, after the Turks had embraced Islam, he fought on their side against the Muslims, when the Islamic government disregarded the teachings of Islam and strayed from the path of its law. The words al-Tabari records give us an insight into the cause to which he devoted himself: “Nothing brings my heart joy except that God should be obeyed.”
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00179

His deeds were true to his words. When Nasr ibn Sayyar, the Umayyad governor of Khurasan, tried to persuade him to abandon the revolt by sending him money, furnishings and horses, al-Harith kept none of them for himself but shared them equally among his followers. He also turned down the promise of a governorship and great wealth — the governor offered him a hundred thousand dinars. Instead, he sent him a letter:
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00181

... I want none of this world, none of its pleasures, nor the chance to marry women from noble Arab families. All I ask for is the Book of God, that the teachings of the Prophet be put into practice, and that good and honourable people be entrusted with public office.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00182

Al-Tabari tells us how simply and modestly he lived: “He would sit on a pack saddle, with a coarse cushion folded for him.” His high principles and genuine chivalry are evident from another account, according to which he forbade his followers to take part in looting, apart from seizing weapons and horses. His movement therefore sought to make the Quran and the Prophet's teachings the guiding principles of government. Its aim was a government acceptable to the majority, one that would put the Islamic ideal of justice into practice.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00183

It is telling that he never laid claim to the caliphate himself, nor received pledges of allegiance as caliph. We therefore believe that the movement of al-Harith ibn Surayj was a political and social revolution expressed through religion, not a product of personal ambition or simply a clash of tribal and ethnic loyalties.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00184

This explains why the rebels were prepared to stop fighting, in spite of their victories, when the caliph appeared willing to meet their demands for justice. Nor did they hesitate to resume the struggle once they realised he had broken his promises. Their guiding principle was that blood should not be shed without just cause.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00185
That principle continued to guide them throughout their wars, which ended only when they were defeated and their leader was killed in 128 AH.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00186

Despite its failure, the revolt of al-Harith is evidence of how thoroughly the Murji'ites had become a revolutionary movement in their own right. It was fundamentally different from the earlier revolts in which they had fought alongside Ibn al-Ashath and Ibn al-Muhallab. The revolt of al-Harith ibn Surayj truly marked a bright period in Murji'ite history, when they took up the social cause and defended it in a genuinely Islamic spirit. It was, in other words, a revolution from below, not from above.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00187

Though the revolt was defeated, it had extremely important positive consequences, some direct and others indirect. After al-Harith was killed, the Umayyad government was forced to abandon some of its oppressive financial policies in Khurasan and adopt a gentler and more moderate approach. These concessions to the will of the rebels were a sign of things to come. The Abbasid movement undoubtedly benefited from the Murji'ite revolt in Khurasan when it brought down the Umayyad caliphate in 132 AH.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00188

It is hardly surprising that the Hashemites, both the supporters of Ali's family and the Abbasids, welcomed the victories the rebels won against the Umayyad governors of Khurasan. Their advocates watched closely as Umayyad power faltered under the rebels' blows. They were able to see where the ruling system was vulnerable and where its military power had failed, and they drew on what they had learned when they launched their own revolution under the leadership of Abu Muslim al-Khurasani. It seems that for a time they considered joining the rebels themselves. But they thought it wiser to wait cautiously and contented themselves with urging al-Harith to press on in his struggle against the Umayyads. We can see this from a poem that al-Kumayt, the poet of the Hashemites, sent from Kufa to al-Harith ibn Surayj. He urged him to fight the Umayyads and apologised for being unable to send men and weapons. Here are some of its lines:
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00190

Carry to the people of Marw, Across all the miles that lie between us, The greeting of a friend who wishes you well And urges you to stand firm in what you have begun. Carry also our apologies to al-Harith: The people here are struggling themselves. Were it not so, you would have more horses From the two cities, galloping to you with their riders. Do not lose heart, or bow to humiliation, And let no one deceive you with a promise. To let yourselves be cheated and accept a scoundrel's oppression Is to be no better than women who sell themselves. Otherwise, raise the black banners Against those who have gone astray and commit injustice.
The Murji'ites: From Defending the Rulers to Revolution
passage-en-00191

And so the Murji'ites, a party of the centre that began with moderation and went on to justify those in power out of self-interest, turned into a movement of opposition demanding reform. In the end it became every bit as revolutionary as the parties of the left. It played a major part in bringing down the Umayyad right, whose rule was finally ended by the Abbasid revolution.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00192
The Abbasids
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00193
Riding the Revolutionary Wave
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00194

We would naturally expect an abundance of historical sources from the Abbasid age. After all, this was a time when people were recording their own history and when science, art and literature flourished. As the machinery of government grew more sophisticated, drawing particularly on Persian experience, so too did the means of preserving official documents. The government offices were packed with countless records, including the papers of the revolution itself. Yet none of these original documents has come down to us.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00195

We believe the Mongol invasion of Iraq was as much to blame for their disappearance as it was for the destruction of the millions of books and reference works held in the library of Baghdad's House of Wisdom. The familiar story of the Mongols crossing the Tigris on a bridge of books and papers may owe much to exaggeration and a vivid imagination. But there can be little doubt about what it conveys: the wanton destruction of the heritage of a flourishing civilisation by a brutal, warlike people.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00196

Even so, the writings of al-Tabari, al-Yaqubi, al-Masudi, Ibn Qutayba and al-Baladhuri remain among our most important sources for this age. Historians today can build a much clearer picture of how the Abbasid period unfolded by reading widely beyond these works, taking in books on Islamic law, religious movements, geography, literature and the lives of notable people.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00197

For our particular study, it is literature — poetry and prose alike — that really comes into its own. We rely on it above all to recover the history of the secret Abbasid movement. Literature can give us a remarkably true picture of the social, cultural and economic life of an age. Sometimes it even offers glimpses into political affairs that are missing from the very sources where we would expect to find them. A good example is the correspondence of government officials and rulers that has survived as literature.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00198

Ahmad Zaki Safwat gathered a wealth of these letters in his well-known collection, Arab Letters from the Golden Ages of Arabic. Its third volume covers the early Abbasid period. It is our main source for shedding light on the organisation of the underground movement just before the Abbasid caliphate was founded in 132 AH. It confirms precise details that we find elsewhere. More importantly, it is the only source rich in otherwise unavailable information about how the underground organisation continued to operate even after the caliphate was established. At the end of this study, we will reproduce selected passages from letters exchanged between the caliphs and the movement's leaders.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00199

The great scholar Ibn Khaldun writes in his Muqaddima (Introduction) that two things are necessary for the rise of a state: a strong sense of solidarity among people and a just cause. A cause without a united body of people to embrace and support it will not achieve its aim. Equally, solidarity alone is not enough to found states with “wide dominions and mighty kingdoms”. A religious cause lends greater strength to that solidarity:
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00201

Religion sweeps away the rivalry and jealousy among people bound together by solidarity, giving them a single direction in their pursuit of what is right. Once they see their cause clearly, nothing can stand in their way. They are all heading in the same direction, they all want the same thing, and they are prepared to give their lives for it.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00202

Ibn Khaldun's theory of how states come into being makes sense up to a point. But if we dig a little deeper, we find that the aims of a movement must go hand in hand with the living conditions and hopes of the people who unite behind it.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00203

Unless a movement — any movement — takes up the demands of ordinary people and gives voice to their hopes, it is bound to fail. And no matter how noble its aims, it will get nowhere without popular support. How many grand ideals and visions of a perfect society have withered and died because they had no roots in the real world and could never be put into practice?
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00204

A just cause alone cannot bring about revolutionary change. Nor can a strong sense of solidarity among people achieve it on its own. What matters is the bond between the two. A revolution succeeds when the principles of the movement answer the needs of the people who rally behind it.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00205

The Abbasid movement succeeded because it embraced justice and raised the banner of equality among people who had long suffered social injustice and ethnic discrimination. I mean the mawali — Muslims from Persia and Khurasan who lived under Arab patronage. What were the actual conditions that made this success possible? That is the question we will now try to answer.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00206

Let us begin with the people who embraced the movement and gave it their strength. What was life like for the Persians and the people of Khurasan under the Umayyads? What place did they occupy in the politics, society, economy and culture of the age?
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00207

The Persians and Khurasanis, heirs to an ancient civilisation, were shut out of government and politics. The Arabs alone held the reins of power. These other peoples lived as a subordinate class, working to support an Arab elite of soldiers and government officials who took the fruits of their labour. Islam called for equality and justice between Arabs and non-Arabs alike, yet the mawali saw a glaring contradiction between the teachings of their religion and the way they were governed in its name. It was this contradiction that made them receptive to any movement that offered deliverance from Umayyad oppression and a return to the social justice prescribed by Islamic law. The new movement was bound to be religious in character, but social in its aims.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00208

Let us look more closely at what happened. In politics, the Umayyad caliphs had departed from Islamic law. They abandoned the democratic principle of consultation and turned the caliphate into a hereditary monarchy, the exclusive possession of the Umayyad family. Most of its members devoted themselves to a life of luxury and indulgence. Men such as Yazid ibn Muawiya, Yazid ibn Abd al-Malik and al-Walid ibn Abd al-Malik preferred drinking wine, pleasure and music to seeing that justice was done and fulfilling their religious duties.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00209

Just as the Umayyads monopolised the caliphate, the Arabs monopolised provincial governorships and military service. Out of this grew a wealthy Arab elite of officials whose fortunes were built at the expense of the mawali. They acquired palaces and estates and embezzled vast sums of tax revenue. Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad, the governor of Iraq, tried to draw on the skills of the Persians and Khurasanis. He turned to the dahaqin, the great landowners, and entrusted some of them with collecting the land tax.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00210

These men did indeed know more about tax collection and were more trustworthy. Yet the arrangement did nothing to stop Arab officials in the eastern provinces extorting money and amassing enormous fortunes. The governors turned a blind eye to the disgraceful conduct of their fellow Arabs, out of loyalty to their own people. The only real result was to revive the class divisions of pre-Islamic Iran. The great landowners regained some of their old power at the expense of the working people. Eager to please their Arab masters and safeguard their new position, they subjected the peasants to ever harsher treatment and heavier financial burdens. Many farmers were driven to abandon their land and move to the towns.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00211

An “Arab military aristocracy” emerged too. Arab soldiers regularly received generous payments from the military pay office, as well as the abundant spoils and revenues they took in their continual raids into the lands of the Turks in Central Asia. Historians tell us that most Persian and Khurasani mawali who fought in these battles were denied their rightful share. This ethnic discrimination, and the departure from the teachings of Islamic law, stirred a number of religious scholars and pious Muslims to speak out. They denounced Umayyad policy and urged the mawali to rise against it.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00212

To make matters worse, Umayyad policy discriminated even among the Arabs themselves. The Quraysh enjoyed a special standing among the tribes because the caliphate belonged to them. Some of the Arab tribes of Khurasan deeply resented this favouritism. One poet gave voice to their feelings:
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00214

Quraysh took the pleasures of life for themselves, And used us to shield them from every dusty pass in Khurasan. Would that Quraysh might wake one night To find themselves swimming in the depths of a green sea!
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00215

In response, the Umayyads deliberately rekindled the old feuds and tribal rivalries between the Arabs of the north and those of the south. Their aim was to prevent the Arab tribes from uniting to dislodge Quraysh from its privileged position, and to maintain a balance of power that would keep the dynasty in office. But the revival of those rivalries damaged Arab political influence in the provinces. War after war broke out between the tribes, bringing turmoil and unrest. Khurasan was especially torn by these conflicts, and its own people suffered in the process. Their resentment towards the Arabs as a whole deepened, and they longed to see the end of Arab rule.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00216

Unjust taxation was one of the chief causes of the Khurasanis' anger at the Umayyad caliphate. Its financial policy was a flagrant violation of Islamic teachings. The authorities continued to levy the jizya, the tax on non-Muslims, on mawali who had embraced Islam. They devised new taxes for them that had no basis in Islamic law. On top of that came the gifts they were required to present to the caliphs, governors and officials at the two festivals of Nowruz and Mihragan. Then there was the humiliation tax collectors inflicted on taxpayers and the brutal treatment of those who could not meet their payments. Abu Yusuf tells us that collectors forced people to carry stones or water jars around their necks, made them stand on one leg for hours, and then bound them so that they could not bow down in prayer.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00217

The ascetic caliph Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz tried to put an end to these injustices. He abolished all the earlier laws and measures and followed Islamic law in his treatment of Muslims and protected non-Muslim communities alike. But he did not live long. His reforms were reversed, and things went back to the way they had been.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00218

For all these reasons, the Persians and Khurasanis came to resent Umayyad rule and its policies. They rose in revolt time and again, but their uprisings lacked organisation and preparation. The Umayyad armies crushed them with brutal force, thanks to a handful of daring Arab commanders utterly devoted to the ruling family and the preservation of “Arab supremacy”. New social developments in Khurasan, however, were paving the way for enormous political changes.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00219

The solidarity that bound the Arabs together had been weakened by the long struggle between the Yemeni and Mudar tribes. Their unity fell apart. They lost their military edge as they settled into lives of ease, luxury and pleasure. Tired of life in the military camps, they abandoned the very source of their strength. Meanwhile, Arabs and mawali had mingled, giving rise to a new generation of mixed ancestry that cared much less about loyalty to Arab blood. The solidarity of the Arabs — the very pillar of the Umayyad state — was cracking, and this hastened the state's downfall at the hands of a new force united in Khurasan. As Ibn Khaldun aptly observed, “When a life of luxury and ease overtakes the people whose solidarity holds a state together, that state begins to grow old.”
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00220

At the same time, class conflict within Persian and Khurasani society itself reached its height. As we have seen, the old class of great landowners had regained its former influence. Besides collecting taxes, its members held important posts in the administration. They had become, in effect, “servants of the ruling power”. The governors naturally used them as informers and spies on their own fellow countrymen, the peasants and farmers. There is no doubt that the lives of the latter grew worse. They were prey to two sets of wealthy masters: the old Persian landowning class and the new Arab elite.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00221

As the financial burden grew, some peasants had no choice but to leave the land and settle in the towns. Some governors forced great numbers of these migrants back to their villages, while others let them be. Some of the migrants went to work for the Arabs; others took up crafts and trades. They made good profits and formed the beginnings of an ambitious new middle class, a bourgeoisie eager to rise to prominence. The growing exodus to the towns, meanwhile, left farms in ruin. Agricultural output fell, and land tax revenues fell with it. The state lost much of its income and was sometimes unable to pay its soldiers. They revolted more and more frequently against their governors, weakening the provincial army.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00222

As peasants continued to pour into the towns, there simply were not enough jobs to go round. Wages fell and unemployment spread. Out of these conditions emerged a discontented working class, the beginnings of a proletariat, whose members joined the underground revolutionary organisations. It is hardly surprising that the wealth and cultural heritage of the new urban middle class made it the leading force in the Abbasid movement. The movement drew its strength from the peasants and oppressed people of the countryside and the angry workers in the towns. They became its loyal foot soldiers. In this way, the conditions in Khurasan were ripe for the seeds of a revolution that was more social in nature than political or religious.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00223
So much for the people who rallied behind the cause. What about the movement itself?
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00224

That brings us to its leading figures, to what drove them to wage their struggle in secret, and then to the movement's slogans and aims. We will also look at how its underground organisation was structured and how it evolved as the movement encountered new difficulties.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00225

One thing needs to be said at the outset. The Abbasid family did not lay the foundations of this movement or sow its seeds. Circumstances alone delivered into their hands the leadership of a carefully built underground organisation, complete with its own branches, organisers and followers. They reaped the harvest that their cousins, the descendants of Ali, had sown. They rode the rising tide of revolution, as the saying goes, and turned their backs on the pioneers who had endured the bitterest trials to build that organisation.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00226

We have already looked at the emergence of political and religious parties in Islam. The Kharijites appeared as a revolutionary, democratic party in the wake of the arbitration dispute. They opposed Ali until his assassination and regarded the Umayyads as usurpers of the caliphate. Their many revolts throughout the second half of the first century AH ended in failure, driving them to take their struggle underground.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00227

The second party, the Shia, remained loyal to Ali ibn Abi Talib. They condemned the Kharijites for rebelling against him and the Umayyads for seizing his rightful place as caliph. After Ali's death, they rallied around his son Hasan. He preferred peace and willingly gave up his claim to put an end to the civil strife. But his decision did not break up the party. Its leaders remained close to Hasan, who urged them to be patient and wait for circumstances to turn in their favour. When Hasan died, the Shia rallied around his brother Husayn. He claimed the caliphate and denounced the Umayyads for turning it into a hereditary monarchy.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00228

Husayn's martyrdom was a victory for the Shia cause. His well-known tragic death fuelled their anger at the Umayyads. The mawali began embracing Shi'ism in large numbers, and the family of Ali came to represent popular opposition to the ruling dynasty. Like the reckless uprisings of the Kharijites, the Shia revolts were social revolutions dressed in religious language. The Umayyads had no qualms about crushing their leaders without mercy. Many members of Ali's family lost their lives, and the Shia went through a terrible ordeal.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00229

After one disaster followed another, the Shia turned away from open rebellion for a time. They adopted a new way of carrying on their struggle through organised underground activity. Their political thinking at the time clearly reflects this change.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00230

It is worth noting how much Shia thought as a whole drew from ancient Persian culture. This tells us a great deal about the role the Persians played in Shi'ism. They were drawn to the movement not simply because of the special standing of the Prophet's family, or because Husayn ibn Ali had married a Persian woman. The family of the Prophet represented the strongest opposition to Umayyad policy, and it had taken up the cause of justice in the true Islamic sense.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00231

There can be no doubt that the Prophet's family understood Islam better than anyone else, was among the most devoted to its principles and was deeply committed to putting its teachings into practice. From their first imam, Ali ibn Abi Talib, they had inherited a tradition of deep religious learning and wide knowledge. Their long experience in exploring every branch of knowledge and drawing on it in the service of their cause is beyond dispute. They saw no harm in adopting many Persian ideas, giving them an Islamic form and using them to support their rightful claim to leadership and to urge people to reclaim it from those who had seized it. It is hardly surprising, then, that Shia underground activity drew on Persian experience of organisation and gave voice to Persian hopes of liberation from social injustice.
The Abbasids: Riding the Revolutionary Wave
passage-en-00232
The imprint of Persian ideas on Shia political thought at this time is particularly striking. As the writer al-Aqqad observes:
